source.title_on_document: The Pedagogical Impact of ChatGPT on High-school Student’s Creative Writing Skills: An Exploration of Generative AI Assisted Writing Tools

paper_design_summary: Eleventh-grade students at Angsilapittayakom School in Thailand were allocated to ChatGPT-integrated or conventional classroom writing lessons; the paper calls the design quasi-experimental but explicitly describes random group allocation (PDF pp. 4-5, printed pp. 20-21). Both groups received 20 hours of instruction and wrote narratives before and after instruction without electronic devices or internet access (PDF pp. 9-10, printed pp. 25-26). The researcher and two native speakers rated the narratives using a creative-writing rubric, with comparative results reported for the total score (PDF pp. 7-12, printed pp. 23-28).

studies.label: Classroom creative-writing instruction and unassisted pretest/posttest

assignment.what_was_assigned: Students were allocated to Group A, ChatGPT-integrated writing lessons, or Group B, conventional writing lessons. The classification follows the explicit random-allocation statements despite the author's quasi-experimental label. Instruction occurred within classroom lessons (PDF pp. 4-6, printed pp. 20-22).
assignment.quote: Employing a simple random sampling method, these students were then allocated into two distinct groups, namely Group A (Experimental Group) and Group B (Controlled Group), each comprising 42 students.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 21), Population and Samples; corroborated by PDF p. 4 (printed p. 20), Methodology, which states that group allocation was conducted randomly.

arms.name: Group A (ChatGPT-integrated lessons)
arms.description: Communicative Language Teaching with ChatGPT available during writing lessons for outlines, drafting, revision, and feedback; 10 lesson plans over 20 hours. Students received introductory training in tool use. Assessments were completed without electronic devices or internet resources (PDF pp. 5-7 and 10, printed pp. 21-23 and 26).

arms.name: Group B (conventional lessons)
arms.description: Conventional Communicative Language Teaching without AI-assisted writing tools; matching 10 lesson plans over 20 hours and the same teaching stages. Assessments were completed without electronic devices or internet resources (PDF pp. 6-7 and 10, printed pp. 22-23 and 26).

participants.exclusions: No exclusions or attrition are stated. The analyzed counts recorded here are explicitly documented for the pretest comparison: Table 2 gives N = 42 in each group. The posttest and paired-analysis tables do not restate their analysis Ns, so these study-level counts do not confirm posttest or complete-pair retention. No intention-to-treat analysis is claimed (PDF p. 10, printed p. 26, Table 2; PDF pp. 11-12, printed pp. 27-28, Tables 3-4).
participants.who: Eleventh-grade students from Angsilapittayakom School, within the Chonburi-Rayong Secondary Educational Service Area, in the second semester of the 2023 academic year (PDF p. 5, printed p. 21, Population and Samples).
participants.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 21), Population and Samples, reports 84 students allocated into groups of 42; PDF p. 10 (printed p. 26), Table 2, gives the analyzed pretest group counts quoted here. Thai context: PDF p. 1 (printed p. 17), Abstract.

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT, paid version; underlying model/version not stated (PDF p. 6, printed p. 22, Research Instruments).
ai_tool.how_used: During structured classroom writing lessons, students had access to ChatGPT to generate outlines, draft text, refine ideas, revise content, and receive feedback. Introductory training covered interface use, prompts, suggestions, and feedback. AI was unavailable during the scored pretest and posttest (PDF pp. 5-7 and 10, printed pp. 21-23 and 26, Research Instruments and Data Collection).

task.description: Write an English narrative based on a researcher-provided prompt; the posttest used a different prompt from the pretest. Example tasks included a short story inspired by an abandoned house, a deserted-island scenario, a journal entry, or a dialogue in a mysterious situation (PDF pp. 7-8 and 10, printed pp. 23-24 and 26).
task.duration: 50 minutes for each assessment; instruction comprised 10 lesson plans over 20 hours per group. Calendar duration is not stated (PDF pp. 5-7 and 10, printed pp. 21-23 and 26).

outcomes.name: Creative writing skills: total rubric score
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Total score of 25 points across five dimensions, each worth 5 points: Creativity, Development, Voice, Literary Devices, and Literary Conventions (PDF pp. 7-9, printed pp. 23-25, Creative Writing Skills Assessment and Table 1; PDF pp. 11-12, printed pp. 27-28, Tables 3-4). Scored by the researcher and two native speakers; the native speakers are not described as professional writing experts. The experts who validated the rubric are distinct from this output-scoring panel (PDF p. 7, printed p. 23, Creative Writing Skills Assessment). The paper does not explain how the raters' scores were combined. Only the total has reported comparative results; the five dimensions below have no separate estimates. Both assessments prohibited electronic devices and internet resources (PDF pp. 7 and 10, printed pp. 23 and 26).
outcomes.delay: Upon completion of the 20-hour teaching intervention; no later follow-up or elapsed delay in days is stated (PDF p. 10, printed p. 26, Data Collection, Post-Learning Assessment).

contrasts.reported: Table 4, posttest total score (25 points): Group A M = 22.72, S.D. = 5.72; Group B M = 19.82, S.D. = 7.42; t = 14.46; Sig. = 0.00*. The footnote reads: "Statistical significance at a 0.01 level." These values are transcribed as printed. Group A N = 42 and Group B N = 42 are stated for allocation and the pretest analysis (Population and Samples; Table 2); Table 4 does not give a posttest-specific analysis N. No standard error, confidence interval, degrees of freedom, or standardized effect is printed.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 12 (printed p. 28), Table 4 and accompanying text; PDF p. 11 (printed p. 27), Data Analysis, Independent Samples t-test; group-count provenance: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 21), Population and Samples, and PDF p. 10 (printed p. 26), Table 2.

contrasts.reported: Table 3, Group A total score (25 points): before integration M = 11.46, S.D. = 7.12; after integration M = 22.72, S.D. = 5.72; paired t = 17.91; Sig. = 0.00*. The footnote reads: "Statistical significance at a 0.01 level." Group A N = 42 is printed in the pretest Table 2; the complete-pair N is not separately stated in Table 3. No paired-difference standard deviation, standard error, confidence interval, degrees of freedom, or standardized effect is printed.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 11 (printed p. 27), Table 3 and Data Analysis, Paired Samples t-test; group-count provenance: PDF p. 10 (printed p. 26), Table 2.

outcomes.name: Creativity rubric dimension
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: A 5-point component of the creative writing assessment. Inventiveness, compelling content, and an original and refreshing perspective on human experience; coded as novelty because the rubric emphasizes inventiveness and originality. PDF p. 8 (printed p. 24), Table 1, Creativity. Scored by the researcher and two native speakers; the native speakers are not described as professional writing experts. The experts who validated the rubric are distinct from this output-scoring panel (PDF p. 7, printed p. 23, Creative Writing Skills Assessment). This dimension was scored within the rubric, but no separate component-level means, tests, effects, or contrasts are reported; Tables 3-4 report only the total (PDF pp. 11-12, printed pp. 27-28). The posttest prohibited electronic devices and internet resources (PDF p. 10, printed p. 26, Post-Learning Assessment).

company_involvement.description: No company involvement is reported. The author is affiliated with Angsilapittayakom School, and the study uses the paid version of ChatGPT; no company funding or support is stated.
company_involvement.locator: PDF p. 1 (printed p. 17), author affiliation; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 22), Research Instruments, paid-version description; no company-involvement disclosure elsewhere in the PDF.

eligibility.reason: The document explicitly states random group allocation and describes individual allocation to ChatGPT-integrated versus conventional classroom instruction, supporting field_rct despite its quasi-experimental label (PDF pp. 4-5, printed pp. 20-21, Methodology and Population and Samples). The study reports 84 people, with 42 per arm in the pretest analysis, exceeding the threshold; posttest-specific Ns are not separately reported (PDF p. 5, printed p. 21; PDF p. 10, printed p. 26, Table 2; PDF pp. 11-12, printed pp. 27-28, Tables 3-4). Human raters score students' narrative outputs, including a creativity dimension (PDF pp. 7-9, printed pp. 23-25, Creative Writing Skills Assessment and Table 1). The posttest expressly prohibits electronic devices and internet resources, so this is after_ai evidence (PDF p. 10, printed p. 26, Post-Learning Assessment).

one_line_finding: The unassisted posttest creative-writing total was 22.72 (S.D. 5.72) after ChatGPT-integrated lessons versus 19.82 (S.D. 7.42) after conventional lessons on a 25-point scale, with t = 14.46 and Sig. = 0.00* reported as printed (PDF p. 12, printed p. 28, Table 4).
open_questions: How many students contributed to each posttest and to the paired analysis? The allocation and pretest counts are explicit, but Tables 3-4 omit analysis Ns and the paper gives no attrition flow (PDF pp. 5 and 10-12, printed pp. 21 and 26-28).

Audit the consistency of the independent-samples t = 14.46 and Sig. = 0.00* with the means, standard deviations, and stated group sizes before quantitative synthesis; all values are retained exactly as printed, without recalculation or correction (PDF p. 12, printed p. 28, Table 4; PDF p. 10, printed p. 26, Table 2).

The quasi-experimental label conflicts with explicit random-allocation wording. The coding follows the latter, but the randomization procedure and allocation concealment are not detailed (PDF pp. 4-5, printed pp. 20-21).

How were the researcher's and native speakers' ratings combined into each student's score? The rubric and inter-rater correlations are described, but the aggregation rule and rater blinding are not stated (PDF p. 7, printed p. 23, Creative Writing Skills Assessment).
notes: All locators give the physical PDF page followed by the printed journal page. Read the complete markdown, including references, and extracted text from all PDF pages; there are no appended materials in the saved PDF and no supplementary-material reference is stated. No shared participant sample, data repository, code repository, or preregistration is reported. Outcomes include the reported composite plus the five explicitly scored rubric dimensions; the dimensions have empty contrast lists because separate results are not supplied, rather than because a null effect was found. Baseline is not a separate outcome or study. The between-group assignment is coded between, with repeated pre/post assessments of the same students. The arm_means_sds_ns availability category refers to printed means/SDs and the documented study/pretest group Ns; it must not be read as confirmation of posttest or paired-analysis Ns. No effect sizes or other statistics were derived, and printed Sig. = 0.00* has not been converted into an exact zero probability.
